cim: AI’s roots lie just north of Berkshire County
cim_eredeti: AI’s roots lie just north of Berkshire County
szoveg_eredeti:
The 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project coined the term AI and helped set the course for decades of computing research

A few days ago, out of curiosity, I asked Google AI to document exactly what AI has accomplished in its lifetime. I did not even know what that lifetime was. Instead of attempting to convey its accomplishments, I stumbled onto an amazing local connection to AI, one that touched my life some 49 years ago. I knew maybe one-tenth of this history, but had no idea that it started just a couple of years after I was born.

What I knew: When I was an employee and community student at Dartmouth College back in the mid-1970s, I knew that every office on the Dartmouth campus had a crude (by today’s standards) and very elementary computer system. It was an all-in-one cast aluminum keyboard and printer on a stand that communicated with a computation center by wire. There was no monitor; it communicated via tractor-fed lined computer paper sitting in a box underneath the machine. You typed in an inquiry, and a response was typed back. I suspect most of that computer paper came from a huge yellow structure in the middle of downtown Cambridgeport, Vermont. This tiny village is part of the town of Rockingham, situated between Saxtons River and Grafton. I also knew that the President of Dartmouth College was John Kemeny, a computer scientist who invented BASIC, the first computer language. That’s it.

What I did not know was that the term ”AI,” or Artificial Intelligence, was coined by Dartmouth assistant math professor John McCarthy. Yes, the term we are all talking about in earnest these days was coined just up the road at Dartmouth in 1955, when I was just two years old. I am 73 now, and I'm just finding out that AI has been around since I was two, and it was conceived locally. What, exactly, started this whole AI thing?

AI began in 1956 at the Dartmouth Summer Conference. Here’s exactly what Google AI had to say about the conference: “Though sometimes mythologized as a highly structured symposium, it functioned more like a casual summer research camp. Roughly 10 main scientists (and several dozen short-term visitors) came and went on their own schedules. Instead of producing a singular, physical breakthrough or a unified coding project, the summer was filled with intense debates over how to build intelligent machines. Here, early divisions first formed, notably between the Symbolists (who believed AI should be coded with strict rules and logic) and the Connectionists (who argued for simulating neurological networks). While the organizers grossly underestimated how long it would take to build true AI — believing significant progress could be made in just one summer — the conference succeeded in establishing a lifelong research agenda and launching the world's very first dedicated AI laboratories.”

The epicenter of that research at Dartmouth was a building near the corner of Elm Street (a couple of buildings behind the Baker Library, the iconic building on the green) and North Main Street, known as the Kiewit Computation Center. I remember it as a low-slung, modern concrete-and-glass building built into the side of an earthen berm. Here’s what Google AI had to say about it: The Kiewit Computation Center at Dartmouth College was established through the leadership of early academic computing pioneers and a major donor. Dartmouth mathematics professors John G. Kemeny and Thomas E. Kurtz drove the center's creation. They revolutionized computer science by co-creating the BASIC programming language and the Dartmouth Time-Sharing System (DTSS), pushing to make computers accessible to ordinary students, not just specialists. Kurtz went on to serve as the center's first director from 1966 to 1975. The center was named after Peter Kiewit, a wealthy construction magnate and Dartmouth alumnus (Class of 1922). He and his wife, Evelyn, provided the critical funding— a gift of $500,000 to $650,000 — to build the facility. The Kiewit Computation Center officially opened and was dedicated on December 2, 1966, to house the college's new $2.5 million General Electric mainframe computer. It served as the hub of Dartmouth's historic computing activities until it was transitioned to the Berry Library and demolished in 2000 to make room for Carson Hall.

AI began in the Connecticut River Valley in Hanover, New Hampshire. Today, we are at a crossroads with Artificial Intelligence. It already impacts our lives in ways we are learning about regularly. It is ushering in a time of great fears and fantastical accomplishments. AI data centers are extremely controversial, and so is the entire premise of AI. It is fascinating to me that it began in a local town we all know.
